title: Misophonia: More Than an Annoyance
summary: Josh and Chuck explore misophonia, a condition in which everyday sounds (chewing, lip smacking, clicking pens, slurping) trigger intense emotional reactions such as anger, anxiety, or disgust. They cover the term's history, including the 2001 first description by Pawel and Margaret Jastreboff, the 2014 taxonomy reorganization, and a 2022 expert committee diagnostic definition. The episode discusses prevalence estimates, the brain research (anterior insular cortex, salience network, myelin findings, genetics), the mirror neuron theory, misokinesia, treatments such as CBT, transdiagnostic therapy, tinnitus retraining therapy with pink noise, exposure therapy debates, and self-management strategies. It ends with a tour announcement at the start and listener mail about the Choctaw Nation's donation to Irish famine relief.

segments.title: Tour announcement
segments.summary: Hosts announce upcoming live shows in Medford MA, Washington DC, New York City, Chicago, Minneapolis, Indianapolis, Durham, and Atlanta, and point to ticket info.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to misophonia
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke around, then introduce misophonia as hatred of sound, a strong emotional reaction to ordinary sounds like chewing, lip smacking, and yawning. Chuck and Josh share their own sound annoyances, such as leaf blowers and ambulance sirens.

segments.title: Personal experiences with trigger sounds
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how sounds bother them, and Josh describes Chuck's daughter as having middling misophonia that she mostly manages.

segments.title: Sound annoyance versus misophonia and the ASMR episode
segments.summary: Chuck distinguishes general loudness annoyance from misophonia's emotional response. The hosts note that people with misophonia criticized the earlier ASMR episode, and they decide not to give examples of trigger sounds.

segments.title: History and recent recognition of misophonia
segments.summary: Misophonia is a new clinical concept. It was first described in 2001, and an expert committee created a clinical definition in 2022. Patients have often been dismissed by clinicians.

segments.title: Jastreboff couple and decreased sound tolerance taxonomy
segments.summary: Pawel and Margaret Jastreboff at Emory studied decreased sound tolerance conditions, including hyperacusis, phonophobia, and misophonia. In 2014 they reorganized the taxonomy, placing phonophobia and hyperacusis under the broader framework with misophonia.

segments.title: Hyperacusis, phonophobia and misophonia distinctions
segments.summary: Hyperacusis is described as a mechanical issue involving the ear, while phonophobia is a fear of loud sounds. Misophonia has a neurobiological and possibly genetic basis. The hosts tease a 'smoking gun' explanation to come.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Brief break before the episode resumes.

segments.title: Internet awareness and symptoms
segments.summary: The 2011 New York Times article by Joyce Cohen and online forums raised awareness. Symptoms include anger, anxiety, disgust, and physical responses such as raised blood pressure, sweating, and chest tightness. Rage episodes are rare and mostly linked to comorbid conditions.

segments.title: Trigger sound patterns and prevalence
segments.summary: Misophonia responses are typically to soft sounds rather than loud ones, and people with it do not have better hearing. Prevalence estimates vary: a 2014 study found 3.2 percent among treatment seekers, while other researchers estimate around 20 percent, with women overrepresented.

segments.title: Brain research, salience network, mirror neurons and genetics
segments.summary: An fMRI study implicated the anterior insular cortex. The hosts propose a salience network hypothesis of overactivity or hyperconnectivity. MRI findings showed excess myelin in the medial frontal cortex. The mirror neuron theory is considered untrue. A GWAS links misophonia with PTSD, anxiety, and depression, suggesting a genetic component.

segments.title: Misokinesia and evolutionary theory
segments.summary: Misokinesia is a reaction to fidgety movements. Jane Gregory of Oxford proposes an evolutionary relic explanation. Reddit posts describe the distress, and mirroring a fidget may help.

segments.title: Contagious effects on relationships and the salience hypothesis
segments.summary: Misophonia can affect work and family relationships, and close family members are often the most likely triggers. The hosts discuss the Olfactory and personal salience theory, and Chuck jokingly names it the Josh Clark salient hypothesis.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Brief break before treatment discussion.

segments.title: Treatment landscape and CBT
segments.summary: Treatment is hit or miss, and many clinicians are uninformed. Cognitive behavioral therapy shows benefit: a 2020 randomized trial found significant improvement in 37 percent of the CBT group versus zero percent of controls. Josh and Chuck warn about quack remedies.

segments.title: Tinnitus retraining therapy, pink noise and exposure therapy
segments.summary: Tinnitus retraining therapy uses wearable devices playing low-level pink or white noise below the trigger threshold, and the Jastreboffs report about 80 percent success. Exposure therapy is controversial, and practitioners advise stopping if an emotional response occurs.

segments.title: Associative therapy and self-management
segments.summary: Jane Gregory has tried pairing trigger sounds with spinning teacup rides to create new associations. Self-management includes noise-canceling headphones, avoiding certain meals, and self-advocacy promoted by Shelagh Hayes Raymond of Misophonia International.

segments.title: Hope for future treatment and podcast tangent
segments.summary: The hosts expect more research and treatment in the future. Josh and Chuck discuss Joyce Cohen versus Joyce Brothers, and Chuck recalls the game show episode.

segments.title: Listener mail: Choctaw Nation and Irish famine
segments.summary: Listener Bob Grace from County Carlow describes the Choctaw Nation's donation to Irish famine relief, the Choctaw-Irish monument, and the scholarship program at University College Cork. The hosts respond.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh close with the sign-off and show credits.
